claims.why: Five files come out of building one program with one type in it, and the count is the whole point of the block. Four of them are not your code.
The assembly is always called Sample.dll, on every platform, because a managed assembly is not a platform specific file and does not get a platform specific name.
The launcher is the one file here whose name changes with the operating system, and this is the pattern that covers both spellings of it.
The launcher cannot start without this file, because it is where the version of the runtime to ask for is written down, so a build that does not produce it produces a program that does not run.
Two timings, the comparison between them, and the address. The timings are what this block is for and the comparison is the only part of them that is true everywhere.

claims.contains: the first one cost at least ten times the rest: True
claims.why: This is the load bearing claim of the whole block and the only one worth gating. Ten is a long way below what any machine actually shows, which is a few hundred, and it is set there so that a slow shared runner does not make a true statement go red.

An address in this process, in this run. The shape is all a page can honestly claim about a number that is different every time the program starts, and it is worth claiming because a zero here would mean the method has no entry point at all.
Three facts about the machine, and none of them belongs on a page that four platforms have to agree on.

Every platform this book supports is sixty four bit, and a great deal of the arithmetic in later lessons assumes it out loud. If this ever goes red, the lessons that add up object sizes are wrong rather than this line.

A three part version, which is what the runtime reports when it is a release rather than a preview. It is checked for shape here because a reader comparing their output with the page needs to know which of the two of you is on something unusual.
